chapter: Joining Carter and Goodman in New York
title: The rhythm section: Al Hall, J.C. Heard and Al Casey
summary: Wilson describes drummer J.C. Heard from Detroit, guitarist Al Casey's four-four swing and the rhythm section as a family.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Give me the names of those guys.

Well, Al Hall was on bas$, and then I heard J.C. Heard in Detroit and brought him to New York, on drums -- J.C. was a swinging little drummer, he was a teenager when he joined my band, and he had never played in a big band in his life, but he was playing with Bill Johnson's band at the Cozy Corner in Detroit, I think it was.
That's right -- the Cozy Corner!
On St. Antoine or Hastings, one of the streets.
And he was swinging, too. But he learned how to play in a big band with me, and he was a swinging drummer.
Uh huh, right.
Incidentally, he stumbled upon a lot
of the techniques that Jo Jones was pioneering in those days.
Right.
There was a similarity in their playing the different things -- Chick Webb and Big Sid and Cozy.
There was a difference. Right.
They had found a few little things, and some similarities, too.
Well, he graduated from your band to Cab's band later.
Yes, uh huh.
Because of that.
Well, my guitar player was one of the best that's ever been, Al Casey.
Oh, God, yes.

Yes, Al Casey is one of the greatest. Of course, in those days, all the players played like what Freddie Green does now, played time, you know, four swinging beats to a measure, and of course, Freddie Green has never been surpassed, but Al Casey was one of the great four-four guitar players, like Allen Reuss.
Uh huh, that's right.
But he had his own touch and his own stroke as to how to play that chord just so and make it swing. Didn't they?
